paragraphs: If the State is a moral person whose life lies in the union of its members, and if its most important concern is its own preservation, it needs a universal, compelling force to move and arrange each part in whatever way is best for the whole. Nature gives each man absolute power over all his limbs. In the same way, the social compact gives the body politic absolute power over all its members. This power, directed by the general will, is what bears the name of Sovereignty, as I have said.

But besides the public person, we have to consider the private persons who make it up, whose life and liberty are by nature independent of it. We must therefore distinguish clearly between the rights of the citizens and those of the Sovereign,[1] and between the duties citizens owe as subjects and the natural rights they should enjoy as men.

I admit that by the social compact each man gives away only that part of his powers, goods and liberty that it matters for the community to control. But it must also be granted that the Sovereign is the sole judge of what matters.

A citizen ought to perform every service he can for the State as soon as the Sovereign demands it. But the Sovereign, for its part, cannot impose on its subjects any fetters that are useless to the community, and cannot even wish to do so. For nothing can happen without a cause, whether by the law of reason or by the law of nature.

The commitments that bind us to the social body are binding only because they are mutual. Their nature is such that in fulfilling them we cannot work for others without also working for ourselves. Why is the general will always right, and why do all constantly will the happiness of each person? Only because everyone thinks of “each” as meaning himself, and thinks of himself when he votes for all. This proves that equality of rights, and the idea of justice that such equality produces, come from the preference each man gives to himself, and so from the very nature of man. It proves that the general will, to be truly general, must be general in its object as well as in its essence: it must come from all and apply to all. And it proves that the general will loses its natural rectitude when it is directed at some particular, determinate object, because then we are judging something foreign to us and have no true principle of equity to guide us.

Indeed, as soon as a question of particular fact or right comes up on a point that no general convention has settled, the matter becomes contentious. The individuals concerned are one party and the public is the other, yet I can see neither the law to follow nor the judge to decide. It would be absurd in such a case to propose referring the question to an express decision of the general will. That decision could only be the conclusion of one of the parties, and so, for the other party, it would be merely an external, particular will, inclined on this occasion to injustice and liable to error. Thus, just as a particular will cannot stand for the general will, the general will changes its own nature when its object is particular, and as a general will it cannot pass judgment on a man or a fact. Take the people of Athens, for instance, when they appointed or removed their rulers, voted honors to one man and penalties on another, and by a multitude of particular decrees carried out all the functions of government without distinction. In those cases the people no longer had a general will in the strict sense. They were acting no longer as Sovereign but as magistrate. This will seem to contradict current views, but I must be given time to set out my own.

From all this it should be clear that what makes a will general is less the number of voters than the common interest that unites them. Under this system each person necessarily submits to the conditions he imposes on others. This admirable agreement of interest and justice gives the common deliberations an equitable character. That character vanishes at once when a particular question is discussed, because there is no common interest to unite the judge’s ruling with the party’s and make them one.

Whichever way we approach our principle, we reach the same conclusion: the social compact sets up such an equality among the citizens that they all pledge themselves on the same conditions and so should all enjoy the same rights. Therefore, by the very nature of the compact, every “act of Sovereignty,” _i.e._ every authentic act of the general will, binds or favors all the citizens equally. The Sovereign recognizes only the body of the nation and makes no distinctions among those who compose it. What, then, strictly speaking, is an act of Sovereignty? It is not an agreement between a superior and an inferior, but an agreement between the body and each of its members. It is legitimate because it rests on the social compact, equitable because it is common to all, useful because it can have no object other than the general good, and stable because it is guaranteed by the public force and the supreme power. As long as subjects submit only to agreements of this kind, they obey no one but their own will. To ask how far the respective rights of the Sovereign and the citizens extend is to ask how far citizens can make commitments to themselves, each with all and all with each.

From this we can see that the sovereign power, absolute, sacred and inviolable as it is, does not and cannot go beyond the limits of the general conventions, and that every man may do as he pleases with whatever goods and liberty these conventions leave him. So the Sovereign never has the right to lay more burdens on one subject than on another, because then the matter becomes particular and falls outside its competence.

Once these distinctions are admitted, it is plainly untrue that individuals make any real renunciation in the social compact. On the contrary, the position they find themselves in as a result of the compact is better than the one they were in before. Instead of a renunciation they have made an advantageous exchange. In place of an uncertain, precarious way of living they have a better and more secure one. In place of natural independence they have liberty; in place of the power to harm others, security for themselves; and in place of their own strength, which others might overcome, a right that social union makes invincible. Their very life, which they have devoted to the State, is constantly protected by it. And when they risk their lives in the State’s defense, what are they doing but giving back what they received from it? What are they doing that they would not do more often, and with greater danger, in the state of nature, where they would inevitably have to fight battles, at risk of their lives, to defend the very means of their survival? All must fight for their country when it needs them, it is true, but then no one ever has to fight for himself. Do we not gain by taking on, for the sake of what gives us security, only some of the risks we would have to run for ourselves as soon as we lost it?
